'I still love you, pal,' Biden told Netanyahu in final phone call
In his last phone call with Benjamin Netanyahu as US president, Joe Biden told the Israeli prime minister, "I still love you, pal", according to a transcript of the conversation obtained by the Jerusalem Post.
Five days before leaving office, Biden told Netanyahu, "You're a good man", and "I admire you."
“You’ve been through hell. I can’t tell you how much I appreciate you and what you’ve been through,” Biden said, according to the transcript. “I know we’ve disagreed on occasion but, you know… I still love you, pal.”
The then-US president continued: “I don’t know how you’ve done it all… Next time I think I have a tough job, I’ll think of you… you’re a good man… I admire you. It took a lot of courage to do what you did.”
The call took place on 15 January 2025, the day a ceasefire and hostage-release agreement between Israel and Hamas was announced.
The transript appears to clash with Biden's own account of his relationship with Netanyahu in his memoir Promise Me, America , which has just been published.
In excerpts reported by Newsweek, the former president accused Netanyahu of having “Trump-like tendencies” and “bending democratic institutions to serve his personal needs.” Biden also described a lack of trust between them and criticised Netanyahu’s attempt to overhaul Israel’s judiciary.

Amnesty calls for RSF drone strikes on el-Obeid to be investigated as war crimes
Amnesty International called on Wednesday for Rapid Support Forces (RSF) drone strikes on el-Obeid in Sudan's North Kordofan state to be investigated as war crimes.
The strikes have hit residential areas and civil infrastructure across the city and its surroundings, killing dozens and disrupting public services.
Amnesty investigated nine RSF drone strikes in el-Obeid and its surroundings, which killed 37 civilians and injured 10 between June and August 2026.
Three of the strikes hit residential areas and four struck key civilian infrastructure, including el-Obeid’s power plant, fuel stations, and the main market. Two targeted moving vehicles in the strategically vital city, which sits on the main route between the capital Khartoum and Darfur in the west.
In all incidents, interviewees told Amnesty they either saw or heard the drones, moments before or after the strikes. Amnesty International’s investigation did not identify military objectives in the vicinity of the sites at the time they were struck.

Jordan gets $6.7bn funding for water desalination project
A desalination project in water-poor Jordan has drawn investment of $6.7 bn and talks are underway to launch similar projects in Syria and Yemen, the head of the UN's Green Climate Fund told Reuters on Wednesday.
The project is the biggest commitment yet by the world's largest multilateral climate fund. It aims to address water stress at a time when the climate crisis is increasing the problem.
Jordan ranks among the countries with the least available water.
Launched officially on Wednesday by Prince Faisal bin Al Hussein, the younger brother of Jordan's King Abdullah II, the Aqaba–Amman Water Desalination and Conveyance Project will eventually move 300 million cubic metres of additional water and serve 40 percent of the population.
Last year, the fund approved $295m in grants and loans that attracted further public and private sector funding to reach a total of $6.7bn.
The Green Climate Fund was set up under the United Nations climate framework to help developing nations adapt and curb their emissions.

Trump's Board of Peace says Gaza ceasefire has delivered 'nothing visible'
US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace, the body supposedly tasked with overseeing the end to fighting in Gaza, has accused both Israel and Hamas of failing to end hostilities, leaving the Palestinian enclave's population in dire need.
The 12-page Board of Peace report, seen by Reuters, is the body's second to the United Nations Security Council since the US-backed ceasefire came into effect 13 months ago. It offers a "sobering assessment of progress made since then", Reuters said.
The board, established and headed by Trump, is expected to present the report's findings to a meeting of the council in New York at the end of November.
“The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process,” the report said, warning that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely.”
Since the ceasefire, Israeli attacks have killed more than 1,431 people, including at least 300 children, and wounded 5,026.
The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and a spokesperson for the political office of Hamas did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the report.
“There is no ceasefire in Gaza. People talk about a ceasefire but at best it’s a reduced fire,” Chris Sidoti, a member of the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, told MEE's Expert Witness podcast this week.

UN migration agency warns of more Gaza hypothermia deaths, as Israel bars 100,000 tents from entering territory
The UN migration agency has warned of further deaths from hypothermia in Gaza as Israel continues to heavily restrict the entry of shelter aid into the territory.
Heavy rains swept through the war-torn enclave last week, inundating thousands of makeshift tents where the majority of Gaza's population is sheltering. A nine-month-old baby died from the cold amid the plummeting temperatures.
"Without proper shelter, without critical relief items, then hypothermia deaths will occur," Karl Baker, head of the International Organization for Migration's Gaza programme, said on Tuesday, adding that children were particularly vulnerable, since they lose body heat more quickly. "It's unacceptable to have hypothermia in the modern world."
Baker said that some 100,000 tents were prepositioned outside Gaza, but the Israeli authorities had barred the entry of items which they consider to be "dual use"- predominantly shelter items including tent poles and mobile homes.
Baker described meeting a drenched family sheltering beneath sagging, worn-out tarpaulins. "Gaza is turning into one large IDP camp (internally displaced persons). It ranks as one of the worst I've walked through," he said.
Reporting by Reuters

"Nabeel defended our rights with dignity and paid a heavy personal price, as did his family, for standing up for the rights of his people," Wadaei wrote on X.

Family of Palestinian journalist Mohammed Atiq demands his release
The family of Palestinian journalist Mohammed Atiq has demanded that his place of detention be disclosed and that he be released, following his arrest by the Israeli army at dawn on Sunday.
Israeli soldiers raided his home in the town of Burqin, west of Jenin, blew open the door, and searched the premises before taking Atiq to an unknown location. His family has yet to receive any information regarding his whereabouts or the conditions of his detention.
Atiq’s arrest comes amid an ongoing campaign of pursuit and detention targeting Palestinian journalists due to their professional work.
The Journalists' Syndicate has reported that approximately 210 journalists including about 23 women have been arrested since 7 October 2023. Meanwhile, the Palestinian Prisoners' Club confirms that 38 journalists, including five women, remain in Israeli occupation prisons.
Atiq works as a photojournalist for several international outlets, including Middle East Eye. About a month ago, he was detained for several hours while filming the olive harvest in the village of Anza, near Jenin.

Britain sanctions Israeli settlement builders, Gaza aid-blocking activists
The British government announced on Tuesday it would impose sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank and an activist group that prevents the delivery of aid to Gaza.
Britain announced asset freezes and director disqualifications on the eight companies including Har Hevron Development Company Ltd, Hemdat Shomron Ltd and S.A.G. (Velvel) Construction and Development Ltd, which construct and develop homes in the West Bank.
The government announced the sanctions package shortly before the final deadlines for the E1 tender, a settlement project which would bisect the Israeli-occupied West Bank and cut it off from East Jerusalem, fragmenting the land Palestinians hope will form the heart of a state.
"Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this Government's approach," the British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said in a statement. "That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution."
The government also imposed sanctions on Tzav 9, a group which it said had regularly blocked humanitarian aid trucks delivering food, water and fuel to the Gaza Strip.
Israel in September threatened to close the British Consulate building in East Jerusalem in response to London’s decision to impose trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
British and Israeli diplomats last month reached a last-minute agreement to avoid the closure of the consulate.
Reporting by Reuters

This year marked a quarter of a century since the beginning of the “war on terror”, and in that time, the British state has built one of the most extensive counter-extremism systems in the world.

It would be easy to treat these as separate stories, one about security and the other about community relations - but a new report from Cage International argues that they are not.
The definition has been shaped so precisely around the security state that, read closely, it functions less as a protection for Muslims than as a protection for the institutions that have spent two decades treating them as suspects.
